trans.sense: something which one has or suspects to have seen or experienced before

examples.text: Why did some déjà vus pattern or pulse at certain peak moments and not others?
examples.ref: 1996, José Argüelles, “The Secret Time Sharers and the Discovery of the Pulsar Code”, in The Arcturus Probe: Tales and Reports of an Ongoing Investigation, Flagstaff, Ariz.: Light Technology Publishing, →ISBN, part one (Launching the Probe), page 11:

examples.text: He had to get back. Soon. All these déjà vus were killing him.
examples.ref: 2005, Lynn Kurland, chapter 27, in Dreams of Stardust, New York, N.Y.: Jove Books, →ISBN, page 271:

examples.text: A few times she mentioned that she’d been having constant déjà vus. She hoped it wasn’t a symptom of a tumor or early-onset dementia.
examples.ref: 2008, Francine Prose, chapter 4, in Goldengrove: A Novel, New York, N.Y.: HarperLuxe, →ISBN, page 83:

glosses: The subjective, unexpected feeling of having experienced something before, especially when that is not the case.

examples.text: Have I done this before? Talk about déjà vu.

glosses: Loosely or humorously, anything one has done before or is being repeated.
